description: Cosmic Cadet is a solo team building a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer. We're creating a fun, interactive app that lets young learners train like an astronaut through simple mission challenges, using real NASA data and facts. Our goal is to make space exploration easy to understand and inspire the next generation of explorers.
summary:
Outpost Commander is a free, two-dimensional web game developed for kids aged 7-12 years that shows what compromises astronauts make when running their Moon outpost. The astronaut travels on the surface of the moon, collects some number of solar energy cells per day, and distributes them between three devices: life support (oxygen supply), a shield generator (to protect from solar flares), and the scientific laboratory (score points). Each cell is used once which introduces the concept of constrained choice. The energy spent on science does not protect the crew from solar flares.

The game represents mission-specific constraints (energy management, life support, and radiation shielding) through gaming mechanics. Every day the space weather depends on a sequence of solar flares based on real data from NASA’s DONKI. Thus, players can see how their decisions about the shields affect damages caused by the solar flares. Different sequences increase replayability of the game. The game uses simple explanations and one-day fact to remain accessible for kids.

The importance of this game is in its ability to teach students about the problems astronauts and mission planners have during deep-space travel.
details:
What it does. Outpost Commander is a free 2D browser game for kids aged 7–12. Players run a Moon base for 10 days. Each morning the solar array makes a few power cells, and the player walks an astronaut from the array to one of three machines: life support (oxygen), the shield generator (radiation protection) or the science lab (points). Each cell can only be used once, so no choice is free. Oxygen use is 16 a day and each cell adds 8, so life support needs about 2 cells a day just to keep oxygen level. Power spent on science cannot protect the crew from a solar flare. At the end of each day a flare streaks in, the shield blocks part of it, and a plain-language report explains what happened and why, plus a short NASA fact.

Real data. The radiation each day is based on real solar flares. The game tries to load recent flares from NASA’s DONKI space weather database, and falls back to real archived 2024 flare dates and classes (such as X9.0 on 3 October 2024). Examples such as minor flares and dust on the panels are labelled as examples, and a Data and sources box credits NASA inside the game.

Benefits and impact. Players see a real constraint of deep space survival instead of reading a poster: power, air and safety compete for the same limited supply, as they do for mission planners. Strong flares are more frequent than in real life so players can practise. Events vary every playthrough, so kids can fail, learn why and try a different plan.

Tools. HTML, CSS and JavaScript with the HTML canvas for the 2D world, Google Fonts, and GitHub Pages for hosting. There is no download, account or special hardware. It works on a computer or phone, with keyboard, on-screen arrows or tap controls. I used the Claude AI assistant to plan the project, write the code and balance the difficulty (details in the AI field).

Creativity and design choices. Walking the astronaut and carrying cells makes the trade-off physical. I limited the game to three simple resources so young players aren’t overwhelmed, avoided any cost-free option, explained terms like solar flare in context, and balanced the difficulty with thousands of simulated playthroughs.
